1 tn The term יֵשׁ (yesh, &quot;there is&quot;) is often used in aphorisms to assert the existence of a particular situation that occurs sometimes. It may indicate that the situation is not the rule but that it does occur on occasion, and may be nuanced &quot;sometimes&quot; (Prov 11:24; 13:7, 23; 14:12; 16:25; 18:24; 20:15; Eccl 2:21; 4:8; 5:12; 6:1; 7:15 [2x]; 8:14 [3x]). 2 tn The noun רָעָה (ra&apos;ah, &quot;evil&quot;) probably means &quot;misfortune&quot; (HALOT 1263 s.v. רָעָה 4) or &quot;injustice, wrong&quot; (HALOT 1262 s.v. רָעָה 2.b); see, e.g., Eccl 2:17; 5:12, 15; 6:1; 10:5. 3 tn Heb &quot;under the sun.&quot; 4 tn The word &quot;weighs&quot; does not appear in Hebrew, but is added in the translation for smoothness. 5 tn Heb &quot;it is great upon men.&quot; The phrase וְרַבָּה הִיא עַל־הָאָדָם (vÿrabbah hi&apos; &apos;al-ha&apos;adam) is taken in two basic ways: (1) commonality: &quot;it is common among men&quot; (KJV, MLB), &quot;it is prevalent among men&quot; (NASB), &quot;that is frequent among men&quot; (Douay). (2) oppressiveness: &quot;it lies heavy upon men&quot; (RSV, NRSV), &quot;it weighs heavily upon men&quot; (NEB, NAB, NIV), &quot;it presses heavily on men&quot; (Moffatt), &quot;it is heavy upon men&quot; (ASV), and &quot;a grave one it is for man&quot; (NJPS). The preposition עַל (&apos;al, &quot;upon&quot;) argues against the first in favor of the second; the notion of commonality would be denoted by the preposition בְּ (bet, &quot;among&quot;). The singular noun אָדָם (&apos;adam) is used as a collective, denoting &quot;men.&quot; The article on הָאָדָם (ha&apos;adam) is used in a generic sense referring to humankind as a whole; the generic article is often used with a collective singular (IBHS 244 §13.5.1f).

6 tn Heb &quot;his appetite.&quot; 7 tn Heb &quot;There is no lack in respect to his appetite&quot;; or &quot;his desire lacks nothing.&quot; 8 tn The verb שָׁלַט (shalat) in the Qal stem means &quot;to domineer; to dominate; to lord it over; to be master of&quot; and in the Hiphil stem &quot;to give power to&quot; (BDB 1020 s.v. שָׁלַט) and &quot;to grant&quot; (HALOT 1522 s.v. שׁלט). God must grant a person the ability to enjoy the fruit of his labor, otherwise a person will not be able to enjoy his possessions and wealth. The ability to partake of the fruit of one&apos;s labor and to find satisfaction and joy in it is a gift from God (e.g., Eccl 2:24-26; 3:13; 5:18 [19]; 9:7). 9 tn Heb &quot;to eat of it.&quot; The verb אָכַל (&apos;akhal, &quot;to eat&quot;) functions as a metonymy of association, that is, the action of eating is associated with the enjoyment of the fruit of one&apos;s labor (e.g., Eccl 2:24-26; 3:12-13, 22; 5:17-19; 8:15; 9:9). 10 tn The phrase &quot;the fruit of his labor&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity. 11 tn Heb &quot;a stranger.&quot; The Hebrew expression אִיש נָכְרִי (&apos;ish nokhri, &quot;stranger&quot;) sometimes refers not to a foreigner or someone that the person does not know, but simply to someone else other than the subject (e.g., Prov 27:2). In the light of 6:3-6, it might even refer to the man&apos;s own heirs. The term is used as a synecdoche of species (foreigner for stranger) in the sense of someone else other than the subject: &quot;someone else&quot; (BDB 649 s.v. נָכְרִי 3). 12 tn Heb &quot;eats.&quot; 13 sn Instead, someone else enjoys it. A person may be unable to enjoy the fruit of his/her labor due to an unfortunate turn of events that robs a person of his possessions (5:13-14) or a miserly, lifelong hoarding of one&apos;s wealth that robs him of the ability to enjoy what he has worked so hard to acquire (5:15-17). Qoheleth recommends the enjoyment of life and the fruit of one&apos;s labor, as God enables (5:18-20). Unfortunately, the ability to enjoy the fruits of one&apos;s labor is often thwarted by the obstacles described in 6:1-2 and 6:3-9. 14 tn Heb &quot;an evil sickness.&quot;

15 tn Heb &quot;the days of his years are many.&quot; 16 tn Heb &quot;he has no burial.&quot; The phrase וְגַם־קְבוּרָה לֹא־הָיְתָה (vÿgam-qÿvurah lo&apos;-haytah, &quot;he even has no burial&quot;) is traditionally treated as part of a description of the man&apos;s sorry final state, that is, he is deprived of even a proper burial (KJV, NEB, RSV, NRSV, ASV, NASB, NIV, NJPS, MLB, Moffatt). However, the preceding parallel lines suggest that this a hyperbolic protasis: &quot;If he were to live one hundred years...even if he were never buried [i.e., were to live forever]....&quot; A similar idea occurs elsewhere (e.g., Pss 49:9; 89:48). See D. R. Glenn, &quot;Ecclesiastes,&quot; BKCOT, 990. 17 tn The noun נֶפֶל (nefel) denotes &quot;miscarriage&quot; and by metonymy of effect, &quot;stillborn child&quot; (e.g., Ps 58:9; Job 3:16; Eccl 6:3); cf. HALOT 711. The noun is related to the verb נָפַל (nafal, &quot;to fall,&quot; but occasionally &quot;to be born&quot;; see Isa 26:18); cf. HALOT 710 s.v. נפל 5. 18 sn The point of 6:3-6 is that the futility of unenjoyed wealth is worse than the tragedy of being stillborn.

1 tn Heb &quot;name.&quot; The Hebrew term שֵׁם (shem, &quot;name&quot;) is used metonymically for a person&apos;s reputation (e.g., Prov 22:1; Deut 22:14, 19; Neh 6:13; also Gen 6:4; 12:2; 2 Sam 7:9; 8:13; 23:18, 22; 1 Chr 5:24; 12:31; 2 Chr 26:15; Neh 9:10; Isa 63:12, 14; Jer 32:20; Ezek 16:14; Dan 9:15); cf. HALOT 1549 s.v. שֵׁם D.2; BDB 1028 s.v. שֵׁם 2.b. 2 tn The comparative term טוֹב (tov, &quot;better&quot;) is repeated throughout 7:1-12. It introduces a series of &quot;Better-than sayings,&quot; particularly in 7:1-6 in which every poetic unit is introduced by טוֹב. 3 tn Heb &quot;good.&quot; The repetition of טוֹב (tov, &quot;good&quot;) forms an inclusion (a structural device that rounds off the unit), while the two internal terms מִשֶּׁמֶן...שֵׁם (shem mishemen, &quot;name ...ointment&quot;) create a paronomastic wordplay (see the note on the word &quot;perfume&quot;). The combination of these two sets of literary devices creates an AB:B&apos;A&apos; chiasm: מִשֶּׁמֶן טוֹב // שֵׁם טוֹב (tov shem // mishemen tov, e.g., &quot;good name&quot;// &quot;ointment good&quot;). 4 tn Or &quot;oil&quot;; or &quot;ointment.&quot; The term שֶׁמֶן (shemen) refers to fragrant &quot;perfume; cologne; ointment&quot; (Amos 6:6; Eccl 10:1; Song 1:2 [1:3 HT]; 4:10); see HALOT 1568 s.v. שֶׁמֶן A.2.c. Bodily oils were expensive (1 Kgs 17:12; 2 Kgs 2:4). Possession of oils and perfumes was a sign of prosperity (Deut 32:8; 33:24; Job 29:6; Prov 21:17; Ezek 16:13, 20). Wearing colognes and oils was associated with joy (Ps 45:8; Eccl 9:8; Isa 61:3) because they were worn on festive occasions (Prov 27:9). The similar sounding terms &quot;name&quot; (שֵׁם, shem) and &quot;perfume&quot; (שֶׁמֶן) create a wordplay (paronomasia). See W. G. E. Watson, Classical Hebrew Poetry (JSOTSup), 242-43; J. J. Glück, &quot;Paronomasia in Biblical Literature,&quot; Semitics 1 (1970): 50-78; A. Guillaume, &quot;Paronomasia in the Old Testament.&quot; JSS 9 (1964): 282-90; J. M. Sasson, &quot;Wordplay in the OT,&quot; IDBSup 968-70. 5 tn The vav prefixed to the form וְיוֹם (vÿyom) functions in a comparative sense, e.g., Job 5:7; 12:11; 16:21; Prov 25:25 (see R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 71, §437). 6 tn The word &quot;one&apos;s&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarity. 7 tn The article prefixed to הַמָּוֶת (hammavet, &quot;death&quot;) probably functions in an indefinite possessive sense or in a generic sense: &quot;one&apos;s death,&quot; e.g., Gen 44:2 (see R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 19, §86, §92). 8 sn There are two ways to understand this proverb: (1) Happy times (characterized by celebration and &quot;fragrant perfume&quot;) teach us less than hard times (&quot;the day of one&apos;s death&quot;) which can bring about moral improvement (&quot;a good reputation&quot;). (2) It is better to come to the end of one&apos;s life (&quot;day of one&apos;s death&quot;) with a good reputation (&quot;a good name&quot;) than to merely be starting life (&quot;day of one&apos;s birth&quot;) in an auspicious manner in joy and wealth (&quot;fine perfume&quot;). Folly and wickedness could foil a good beginning so that a person ends life as a fool. For example, Solomon began as the wisest man who ever lived, only to end life as one of history&apos;s greatest fools.

9 tn Heb &quot;house of mourning.&quot; The phrase refers to a funeral where the deceased is mourned. 10 tn Heb &quot;house of drinking&quot;; or &quot;house of feasting.&quot; The Hebrew noun מִשְׁתֶּה (mishteh) can denote (1) &quot;feast; banquet,&quot; occasion for drinking-bouts (1 Sam 25:36; Isa 5:12; Jer 51:39; Job 1:5; Esth 2:18; 5:14; 8:17; 9:19) or (2) &quot;drink&quot; (exilic/postexilic - Ezra 3:7; Dan 1:5, 8, 16); see HALOT 653 s.v. מִשְׁתֶּה 4; BDB 1059 s.v. שָׁתַה. sn Qoheleth recommended that people soberly reflect on the brevity of life and the reality of death (It is better to go to a house of mourning) than to waste one&apos;s life in the foolish pursuit of pleasure (than to go to a house of banqueting). Sober reflection on the brevity of life and reality of death has more moral benefit than frivolous levity. 11 tn Heb &quot;it&quot;; the referent (&quot;death&quot;) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 12 tn Heb &quot;the end.&quot; The noun סוֹף (sof) literally means &quot;end; conclusion&quot; (HALOT 747 s.v. סוֹף 1; BDB 693 s.v. סוֹף). It is used in this context in reference to death, as the preceding phrase &quot;house of mourning&quot; (i.e., funeral) suggests. 13 tn Heb &quot;all men&quot; or &quot;every man.&quot; 14 tn The imperfect tense verb יִתֵּן, yitten (from נָתָן, natan, &quot;to give&quot;) functions in a modal sense, denoting obligation, that is, the subject&apos;s obligatory or necessary conduct: &quot;should&quot; or &quot;ought to&quot; (see R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 31-32, §172; IBHS 508-9 §31.4g). 15 tn The word &quot;this&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for smoothness.

16 tn NEB suggests &quot;grief&quot;; NJPS, &quot;vexation.&quot; 17 tn Heb &quot;in sadness of face there is good for the heart.&quot; 18 tn Or possibly &quot;Though the face is sad, the heart may be glad.&quot;

J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 47, §261; IBHS 202-4 §11.2.9b). 2 tn The definite article on הֶחָכָם (hekhakham, &quot;wise man&quot;) may be taken in an individualizing (&quot;the wise man&quot;) or generic sense (&quot;a wise man&quot;). 3 tn Or &quot;the explanation.&quot; The noun פֵּשֶׁר (pesher) denotes &quot;solution; explanation; interpretation; meaning&quot; (HALOT 982-83 s.v. פֵּשֶׁר; BDB 833 s.v. פֵּשֶׁר). The Hebrew term is an Aramaic loanword from פִּשְׁרָא (pishra&apos;, &quot;diagnosis; meaning; solution&quot;). The Aramaic noun פְּשַׁר (pÿshar, &quot;interpretation of a dream or prophecy&quot;) and verb פְּשַׁר (pÿshar, &quot;to interpret a dream or prophecy&quot;) reflect a later meaning not present in Ecclesiastes, but current at the time of Daniel (Dan 2:5-7; 4:3, 15, 16; 5:12, 15, 16; 7:16) and Qumran (e.g., 1QpHab). 4 tn Heb &quot;a thing.&quot; 5 tn Heb &quot;makes his face shine.&quot; 6 tc The MT vocalizes the consonantal form ישנא as יְשֻׁנֶּא (yÿshunne&apos;, Pual imperfect 3rd person masculine singular from I שָׁנָה, shana, &quot;to change&quot;). However, the LXX μισθήσεται (misqhsetai) reflects an alternate vocalization tradition of יִשָּׂנֵא (yissane&apos;, Niphal imperfect 3rd person masculine singular from שָׂנֵא, sane&apos;, &quot;to hate&quot;), while the Vulgate&apos;s commutabit reflects יְשַׁנֶּה (yÿshanneh, Piel imperfect 3rd person masculine singular from II שָׁנָה, shanah, &quot;to repeat&quot;). tn Heb &quot;the strength of his face is changed.&quot; 7 tn Heb &quot;the strength of his face is changed.&quot; The expression עֹז פָּנָיו (&apos;oz panayv, &quot;strength of his face&quot;) is an idiom for &quot;boldness; impudence&quot; (BDB 739 s.v. עֹז 4) or &quot;hard face&quot; = harsh countenance (HALOT 805 s.v. I עֹז 1.c).

8 tc The Leningrad Codex (the basis of BHS) reads אֲנִי (&apos;ani, 1st person common singular independent personal pronoun): &quot;I obey the king&apos;s command.&quot; Other medieval Hebrew mss and all the versions (LXX, Vulgate, Targum, Syriac Peshitta) preserve an alternate textual tradition of the definite accusative marker אֶת־ (&apos;et) introducing the direct object: אֶת־פִּי־מֶלֶךְ שְׁמוֹר (&apos;et-pi-melekh shÿmor, &quot;Obey the command of the king&quot;). External evidence supports the alternate textual tradition. The MT is guilty of simple orthographic confusion between similar looking letters. The BHS editors and the Hebrew Old Testament Text Project adopt אֶת־ as the original reading. See D. Barthélemy, ed., Preliminary and Interim Report on the Hebrew Old Testament Text Project, 3:582-83. 9 tn The phrase &quot;you took&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for smoothness. 10 tn The genitive-construct שְׁבוּעַת אֱלֹהִים (shÿvu&apos;at &apos;elohim, &quot;an oath of God&quot;) functions as a genitive of location (&quot;an oath before God&quot;) or an adjectival genitive of attribute (&quot;a supreme oath&quot;). 11 tn The words &quot;to be loyal to him&quot; do not appear in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarification.

1 tn Heb &quot;I laid all this to my heart.&quot; 2 tn The term וְלָבוּר (velavur, conjunction + Qal infinitive construct from בּוּר, bur, &quot;to make clear&quot;) denotes &quot;to examine; to make clear; to clear up; to explain&quot; (HALOT 116 s.v. בור; BDB 101 s.v. בּוּר). The term is related to Arabic baraw &quot;to examine&quot; (G. R. Driver, &quot;Supposed Arabisms in the Old Testament,&quot; JBL 55 [1936]: 108). This verb is related to the Hebrew noun בֹּר (bor, &quot;cleanness&quot;) and adjective בַּר (bar, &quot;clean&quot;). The term is used in the OT only in Ecclesiastes (1:13; 2:3; 7:25; 9:1). This use of the infinitive has a connotative sense (&quot;attempting to&quot;), and functions in a complementary sense, relative to the main verb. 3 tn The words &quot;I concluded that&quot; do not appear in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarity. 4 tn Heb &quot;whether love or hatred.&quot; 5 tn Heb &quot;man does not know anything before them.&quot;

6 tn Heb &quot;all things just as to everyone, one fate.&quot; 7 tc The MT reads simply &quot;the good,&quot; but the Greek versions read &quot;the good and the bad.&quot; In contrast to the other four pairs in v. 2 (&quot;the righteous and the wicked,&quot; &quot;those who sacrifice, and those who do not sacrifice,&quot; &quot;the good man...the sinner,&quot; and &quot;those who make vows...those who are afraid to make vows&quot;), the MT has a triad in the second line: לַטּוֹב וְלַטָּהוֹר וְלַטָּמֵא (lattov vÿlattahor vÿlattame&apos;, &quot;the good, and the clean, and the unclean&quot;). This reading in the Leningrad Codex (ca. a.d. 1008) - the basis of the BHS and BHK publications of the MT - is also supported by the Ben Asher text of the First Rabbinic Bible (&quot;the Soncino Bible&quot;) published in a.d. 1488-94. On the other hand, the Greek version in B (Aquila) has two pairs: τῷ ἀγαθῷ καὶ τῷ κακῷ, καὶ τῷ καθαρῷ καὶ τῷ ἀκαθάρτῳ (&quot;the good and the bad, and the clean and the unclean&quot;). Either Aquila inserted καὶ τῷ κακῷ (kai tw kakw, &quot;and the bad&quot;) to fill out a pair and to create six parallel pairs in v. 2, or Aquila reflects an early Hebrew textual tradition tradition of לַטּוֹב וְלַרָע (lattov vÿlara&apos;, &quot;the good and the bad&quot;). Since Aquila is well known for his commitment to a literal - at times even a mechanically wooden - translation of the Hebrew, with no room for improvisation, it is more than likely that Aquila is reflecting an authentic Hebrew textual tradition. Aquila dates to a.d. 130, while the Leningrad Codex dates to a.d. 1008; therefore, the Vorlage of Aquila might have been the original Hebrew textual tradition, being much earlier than the MT of the Leningrad Codex. The alternate textual tradition of Aquila is also seen in the Syriac and Latin versions (but these are dependent upon the Greek = Aquila). On the other hand, the editors of BHK and BHS suggest that the presence of the anomalous לַטּוֹב was an addition to the Hebrew text, and should be deleted. They also suggest that the Greek pair τῷ ἀγαθῷ καὶ τῷ κακῷ (tw agaqw kai tw kakw, &quot;the good and the bad&quot;) does not reflect an alternate textual tradition, but that their Vorlage contained only לַטּוֹב: the Greek version intentionally added καὶ τῷ κακῷ (kai tw kakw, &quot;and the bad&quot;) to create a pair. The English versions are divided. Several follow the Greek: &quot;the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean&quot; (NEB, NAB, RSV, NRSV, NIV, Moffatt, NLT). Others follow the Hebrew: &quot;the good and the clean and the unclean&quot; (KJV, ASV, MLB, NJPS). None, however, delete &quot;the good&quot; (לַטּוֹב) as suggested by the BHK and BHS editors. If the shorter text were original, the addition of καὶ τῷ κακῷ would be intentional. If the longer text were original, the omission of וְלַרָע (&quot;and the bad&quot;) could have caused by unintentional homoioarcton (&quot;similar beginning&quot;) in the three-fold repetition of לט in וְלַרָע וְלַטָּהוֹר וְלַטָּמֵא לַטּוֹב (lattov vÿlara&apos; vÿlattahor vÿlattame&apos;, &quot;the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean&quot;). The term וְלַרָע (&quot;and the bad&quot;) was accidentally omitted when a scribe skipped from the first occurrence of לט in לַטּוֹב to its second occurrence in the word וְלַטָּהוֹר (&quot;the clean&quot;). 8 tn Heb &quot;As is the good (man), so is the sinner.&quot;

9 tn Heb &quot;evil.&quot; 10 tn Heb &quot;under the sun.&quot; 11 tn The term &quot;awaits&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for smoothness and stylistic reasons. 12 tn Heb &quot;also the heart of the sons of man.&quot; Here &quot;heart&quot; is a collective singular. 13 tn Heb &quot;and after that [they go] to [the place of] the dead.&quot;

1 tn Heb &quot;flies of death.&quot; The plural form of &quot;flies&quot; (זְבוּבֵי, zÿvuve) may be taken as a plural of number (&quot;dead flies&quot;) or a distributive plural referring to one little fly (&quot;one dead fly&quot;). The singular form of the following verb and the parallelism support the latter: &quot;one little fly...so a little folly.&quot; 2 tn The verb בָּאַשׁ (ba&apos;ash) means &quot;to cause to stink; to turn rancid; to emit a stinking odor&quot; (e.g., Exod 16:24; Ps 38:6; Eccl 10:1); see HALOT 107 s.v. באשׁ 1; BDB 93 s.v. בָּאַשׁ. It is related to the noun בְּאשׁ (bÿ&apos;osh, &quot;stench&quot;; Isa 34:3; Joel 2:20; Amos 4:10); cf. HALOT 107 s.v. באשׁ; BDB 93 s.v. בְּאשׁ. The verbal root נבע means &quot;to ferment&quot; or &quot;to emit; to pour out; to bubble; to belch forth; to cause to gush forth&quot; (HALOT 665 s.v. נבע; BDB 615 s.v. נָבַע). The two terms יַבְאִישׁ יַבִּיעַ (yav&apos;ish yabbia&apos;, &quot;to stink&quot; and &quot;to ferment&quot;) create a hendiadys: a figurative expression in which two terms are used to connote one idea: &quot;makes a rancid stench.&quot; Several versions treat this as a hendiadys (Old Greek, Symmachus, Targum, Vulgate); however, the Syriac treats them as separate verbs. Most translations treat these as a hendiadys: &quot;Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savor&quot; (KJV); &quot;Dead flies make a perfumer&apos;s oil stink&quot; (NASB); &quot;dead flies give perfume a bad smell&quot; (NIV); &quot;Dead flies make the perfumer&apos;s ointment give off an evil odor&quot; (RSV); Dead flies make the perfumer&apos;s ointment give off a foul odor&quot; (NRSV); &quot;Dead flies cause a perfumer&apos;s perfume to send forth a stink&quot; (YLT); &quot;Dead flies make the perfumer&apos;s ointment give off a foul odor&quot; (NRSV). Others render both separately: &quot;Dead flies make the perfumer&apos;s sweet ointment rancid and ferment&quot; (NEB); &quot;Dead flies turn the perfumer&apos;s ointment fetid and putrid&quot; (NJPS). 3 tn Heb &quot;carries more weight than&quot;; or &quot;is more precious than.&quot; The adjective יָקָר (yaqar) denotes &quot;precious; valuable; costly&quot; (HALOT 432 s.v. יָקָר 2) or &quot;weighty; influential&quot; (BDB 430 s.v. יָקָר 4). The related verb denotes &quot;to carry weight,&quot; that is, to be influential (HALOT 432 s.v. יָקָר 2). The idea is not that a little folly is more valuable than much wisdom; but that a little folly can have more influence than great wisdom. It only takes one little mistake to ruin a life of great wisdom. The English versions understand it this way: &quot;so a little foolishness is weightier than wisdom and honor&quot; (NASB); &quot;so a little folly outweighs massive wisdom&quot; (NJPS); &quot;so a little folly outweighs an abundance of wisdom&quot; (MLB); &quot;so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor&quot; (RSV, NRSV, NIV); &quot;so can a little folly make wisdom lose its worth&quot; (NEB); &quot;so a little folly annuls great wisdom&quot; (ASV); &quot;a single slip can ruin much that is good&quot; (NAB); &quot;so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honor&quot; (KJV). The LXX rendered the line rather freely: τιμιον ὀλιγον σοφιἀ ὑπερ δοξαν ἀφροσυνης μεγαλην (&quot;a little wisdom is more precious than great glory of folly&quot;). This does not accurately represent the Hebrew syntax. sn Qoheleth creates a wordplay by using two Hebrew words for social honor or influence: &quot;weighty&quot; = honorable (יָקָר, yaqar) and &quot;heavy&quot; = honor (כָּבוֹד, cavod). 4 tn The MT reads מֵחָכְמָה מִכָּבוֹד (mekhokhmah mikkavod, &quot;more than wisdom, more than honor&quot;), but several medieval Hebrew mss read וּמִכָּבוֹד מֵחָכְמָה (mekhokhmah umikkavod, &quot;more than wisdom and honor&quot;). However the textual problem is resolved, the two nouns form a hendiadys: two terms joined by vav that describe one concept. The first noun retains its full nominal sense, while the second functions adjectivally: &quot;heavy wisdom&quot; or better, &quot;great wisdom.&quot;

5 tn Heb &quot;a wise man&apos;s heart is at his right hand.&quot; The phrase &quot;right hand&quot; is a Hebrew idiom for the place of protection (e.g., Pss 16:8; 110:5; 121:5). In ancient warfare, the shield of the warrior on one&apos;s right-hand side protected one&apos;s right hand. Qoheleth&apos;s point is that wisdom provides protection (e.g., Eccl 7:12). 6 tn Heb &quot;and the heart of a fool is at his left hand.&quot; The fool lacks the protection of wisdom which is at the right-hand side of the wise man (see note on &quot;right hand&quot; in the previous line). The wise man&apos;s heart (i.e., good sense) protects him, but the fool is always getting into trouble.

7 tn Heb &quot;he lacks his heart.&quot; 8 tn Heb &quot;he tells everyone.&quot; 9 sn A fool&apos;s lack of wisdom is obvious to everyone, even when he is engaged in the simple, ordinary actions of life.

1 tn The verb שָׁלַח (shalakh, &quot;to send; to cast&quot;) refers to the action of sending something to someone (e.g., Neh 8:12; HALOT 1995 s.v. שׁלח). The term is traditionally rendered here as &quot;cast&quot; (KJV, NAB, RES, ASV, NASB, NIV); however, some render it &quot;send&quot; (NJPS, NRSV, NEB). LXX uses ἀπόστειλον (aposteilon, &quot;send&quot;). 2 tn Heb &quot;your bread.&quot; The term לֶחֶם (lekhem) is traditionally rendered &quot;bread&quot; (KJV, NAB, RSV, NRSV, ASV, NASB, NIV, NJPS). However, 11:1-2 seems to deal with exporting goods overseas (D. R. Glenn, &quot;Ecclesiastes,&quot; BKCOT, 1002-3). It is better to take לֶחֶם (&quot;bread&quot;) as a metonymy of product, standing for the grain and wheat from which bread is produced (e.g., Gen 41:54-55; 47:13, 15, 17, 19; 49:20; Num 15:19; 2 Kgs 18:32; Isa 28:28; 30:23; 36:17; 55:10; Jer 5:17; Ezek 48:18; Job 28:5; Ps 104:14; Prov 28:3); see HALOT 526 s.v. 1; BDB 537 s.v. 1.b. It is taken this way by several translations: &quot;grain&quot; (NEB) and &quot;goods&quot; (Moffatt). Qoheleth encouraged the export of grain products overseas in international trade. 3 tn Heb &quot;upon the surface of the waters.&quot; This is traditionally viewed as extolling generosity from which a reward will be reaped. On the other hand, some scholars suggest that the imagery deals with commercial business through maritime trade. M. Jastrow took this verse as advice to take risks in business by trusting one&apos;s goods or ships that will after many days return with a profit (A. Cohen, The Five Megilloth [SoBB], 181). Sea trade was risky in the ancient Near East, but it brought big returns to its investors (e.g., 1 Kgs 9:26-28; 10:22; Ps 107:23); see D. R. Glenn, &quot;Ecclesiastes,&quot; BKCOT, 1002-3. The verse is rendered thus: &quot;Send your grain across the seas, and in time you will get a return&quot; (NEB); or &quot;Trust your goods far and wide at sea, till you get a good return after a while&quot; (Moffatt). 4 tn Heb &quot;find it.&quot;

5 tn Heb &quot;give a portion.&quot; 6 tn The phrase &quot;seven or eight&quot; is a graded numerical saying depicting an indefinite plurality: &quot;The collocation of a numeral with the next above it is a rhetorical device employed in numerical sayings to express a number, which need not, or cannot, be more exactly specified. It must be gathered from the context whether such formulae are intended to denote only an insignificant number (e.g., Is 17:6 &quot;two&quot; or at the most &quot;three&quot;) or a considerable number (e.g., Mi 5:4). Sometimes, however, this juxtaposition serves to express merely an indefinite total, without the collateral idea of intensifying the lower by means of the higher number&quot; (GKC 437 §134.s). Examples: &quot;one&quot; or &quot;two&quot; (Deut 32:30; Jer 3:14; Job 33:14; 40:5; Ps 62:12); &quot;two&quot; or &quot;three&quot; (2 Kgs 9:32; Isa 17:6; Hos 6:2; Amos 4:8; Sir 23:16; 26:28; 50:25); &quot;three&quot; or &quot;four&quot; (Jer 36:23; Amos 1:3-11; Prov 21:19; 30:15, 18; Sir 26:5); &quot;four&quot; or &quot;five&quot; (Isa 17:6); &quot;six&quot; or &quot;seven&quot; (Job 5:19; Prov 6:16); &quot;seven&quot; or &quot;eight&quot; (Mic 5:4; Eccl 11:2). 7 tn The word &quot;investments&quot; is not in the Hebrew text; it is added here for clarity. This line is traditionally understood as an exhortation to be generous to a multitude of people (KJV, NAB, ASV, NASB, RSV, NRSV, NIV, NJPS); however, it is better taken as shrewd advice to not commit all one&apos;s possessions to a single venture (A. Cohen, The Five Megilloth [SoBB], 181). D. R. Glenn (&quot;Ecclesiastes,&quot; BKCOT, 1003) writes: &quot;In view of the possibility of disaster, a person should make prudent investments in numerous ventures rather than put all his &apos;eggs in one basket&apos; (e.g., Gen 32:7-8 for a practical example of this advice).&quot; Several translations reflect this: &quot;Divide your merchandise among seven ventures, eight maybe&quot; (NEB); &quot;Take shares in several ventures&quot; (Moffatt). 8 sn The phrase you do not know is repeated throughout this section (11:2, 5-6). Human beings are ignorant of the future. This should motivate a person to invest their financial resources wisely (11:1-3) and to work diligently (11:4-6). 9 tn The term רעה (lit. &quot;evil&quot;) refers to calamity (e.g., Eccl 5:13; 7:14; 9:12).

1 tn The imperative זְכֹר (zekhor, &quot;Remember!&quot;) is a figurative expression (metonymy of association) for obeying God and acknowledging his lordship over one&apos;s life (e.g., Num 15:40; Deut 8:18; Pss 42:6-7; 63:6-8; 78:42; 103:18; 106:7; 119:52, 55; Jer 51:50; Ezek 20:43; Jonah 2:7; Mal 4:4). The exhortation to fear God and obey his commands in 12:13-14 spells out what it means to &quot;remember&quot; God. 2 tn The temporal adjective עַד (&apos;ad, &quot;before&quot;) appears three times in 12:1-7 (vv. 1b, 2a, 6a). Likewise, the temporal preposition בְּ (bet, &quot;when&quot;) is repeated (vv. 3a, 4b). These seven verses comprise one long sentence in Hebrew: The main clause is 12:1a (&quot;Remember your Creator in the days of your youth&quot;), while 12:1b-7 consists of five subordinate temporal clauses (&quot;before...before...when...when...before...&quot;). 3 tn The adjective רָעָה (ra&apos;ah, &quot;evil&quot;) does not refer here to ethical evil, but to physical difficulty, injury, pain, deprivation and suffering (e.g., Deut 31:17, 21; 32:23; 1 Sam 10:19; Neh 1:3; 2:17; Pss 34:20; 40:13; 88:4; 107:26; Eccl 11:10; Jer 2:27; Lam 3:38); see HALOT 1263 s.v. רָעָה 4.b; BDB 949 s.v. רָעָה 2.

4 tn Heb &quot;the light and the moon and the stars.&quot; The phrase &quot;the light and the moon&quot; is a hendiadys (two separate terms denoting one idea) or perhaps even a hendiatris (three separate terms denoting one idea) for &quot;the light of the moon and stars&quot; (e.g., Gen 1:14). 5 tn The verb שׁוּב (shuv, &quot;to return&quot;) here denotes &quot;to desist&quot; (HALOT 1430 s.v. שׁוּב 3). It pictures the disappearance of the clouds as a result of the precipitation of their contents.

6 tn Heb &quot;the watchers of the house.&quot; 7 tn The verb זְוּעַ (zÿua&apos;, &quot;to tremble&quot;) probably does not refer to physical tremors but to trembling in fear (e.g., Esth 5:9; Hab 2:7; Sir 48:12); cf. HALOT 267 s.v. זוע). At the onset of old age, those who had been the most courageous during their youth suddenly become fearful. 8 tn The verb עָוַת (&apos;avat, &quot;to bend; to stoop&quot;) means &quot;to be stooped&quot; (HALOT 804 s.v. עות) rather than &quot;to bend themselves&quot; (BDB 736 s.v. עות). The perfect tense may be taken in an ingressive sense (&quot;begin to stoop over&quot;). 9 tn The term הַטֹּחֲנוֹת (hattokhanot, Qal active participle feminine plural from טָחַן, takhan, &quot;to grind&quot;) is a double entendre. In its literal sense, it refers to female mill-grinders; in its figurative sense, it refers to molar teeth (HALOT 374 s.v. *טֹחֲנָה). The related Hebrew noun טַחֲנָה (takhanah) refers to a &quot;mill,&quot; and the related Arabic noun tahinat means &quot;molar tooth&quot; (HALOT 374 s.v. *טַחֲנָה). 10 tn The verb חָשַׁךְ (khashakh, &quot;to grow dim&quot;) is used elsewhere in reference to failing eyesight (e.g., Ps 69:24; Lam 5:17); see HALOT 361 s.v. חשׁך 2. Therefore, the phrase &quot;those who look through the windows&quot; is probably a figurative description of the eyes, picturing failing eyesight at the onset of old age.
